utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, can you make sure that the witness is brought in, please? (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. Good morning to counsel for the Prosecution. Good morning to counsel for Defence. Good morning to you, General Blaskic. I am just reminding the public that General Blaskic is now a witness. Mr. Blaskic has chosen to be a witness in his own trial. He is under oath, and he is in the middle of cross-examination. Mr. Registrar, we have noted this morning again that there was some delay in the transport of the witness. What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. There has been a slight problem, it is true, but it is not the security service of the Tribunal which is responsible for this delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Then I was wrong then. I'm so sorry I said that, and I see it's a huge secret what actually happened to the witness on his way here. Good morning, Mr. Kehoe, and the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could ask that the witness be given 456/8 back. Mr. President, this is the cease-fire order of the 27th January, 1993, and with the assistance of the usher, I believe we have a corrected translation in the record now which carries with it the time on the order of 17.40, and that's in both the English and the French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. So it's 17.40 on January 27, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These two new exhibits which were used yesterday and which bear the right time will be Prosecution Exhibit 456/8A and 456/8A bis so that we can take into account what corrections have been brought to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. 456/8A bis. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, these particular negotiations that you were engaged in on the 27th of January, 1993, where did they take place?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, these negotiations took place at the UNPROFOR headquarters for Bosnia-Herzegovina in Kiseljak. May I just correct myself --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, please, General -- well, if you want to correct yourself, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, please. General, please answer the question. The question is very precise. Let's not start to make comments on what has been put to you. You are the witness. A question is put to you. You can give a very clear and precise answer to that question. Either you remember or you don't. Either you know or you don't. We are not each time going to go through a series of comments. You know that time is very precious to the Prosecution right now, so please try to give a very clear answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, how far is the U.N. headquarters in Kiseljak from the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is about 600 to 700 metres away, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Kiseljak barracks is where the headquarters of the Ban Jelacic Brigade was; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the barracks, it was the command of the Ban Jelacic Brigade which would be mobilised according to need, so it wasn't a live brigade, so to speak. But people would live at home and, if necessary, they would be mobilised. When they weren't mobilised, they were civilians, farmers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The document that you have before you, Exhibit 456/8, has a deadline for the implementation of the cease-fire of 28 January, 1993 at 00.01.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was the document, and that was the deadline which had been reached by agreement between me and the 1st and 3rd Corps with the mediation of Brigadier Simpson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn, General, to Prosecutor's Exhibit 510.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting for this Prosecutor's Exhibit, may I just say a word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please do, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was not my intention a moment ago to expand my answer to the question. Yesterday, I made a mistake when I spoke about the shifts leaving from the municipality of Travnik to the front line against the Serbs. I looked through my chronology more carefully, and in the chronology, it states the 27th of November, 1992, and I said yesterday that it was the 17th of November, 1992. That was the answer I gave yesterday. So it was a ten-day difference, and I merely wanted to correct that error and say that it was the 27th of November, 1992, that is my chronology, when the units from all the municipalities went to the Travnik front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for correcting this error. It will be taken down in the transcript anyway, so you are quite right to correct what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this is an order that is issued by the commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, Mijo Bozic, on the 27th of January, 1993, and it is an order for offensive combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could the ELMO be switched on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of this document, the commander, Mijo Bozic, orders the 1st Company and the 1st Battalion to be "mobilised immediately, reinforced with the anti-sabotage platoon and transferred to the village of Datici by APC where they shall be deployed in combat positions." It gives the various villages to be disarmed and notes: "After completing fire preparations, proceed to disarm the villages of Radeljevici, Pobrdze, Markovici, Maslinovici. "Be ready time at initial positions at 16.00 hours. "Be ready to open MB /mortar fire/ at 16.00 hours. "Fire preparations to be carried out from 16.00 to 16.30 with 10 82mm and 120mm MB shells each, selecting targets within the villages. "2. After the preparation has been completed, the local population is to be called to surrender unconditionally all weapons; otherwise the village will be burnt to the ground. In case of refusal to surrender arms open strong and concentrated fire on all targets with PAT /anti-aircraft gun/, PAM /anti-aircraft machine-guns/, and MB /mortars/ and proceed with mopping up the area. "3. After these villages have been taken the enemy is to be pushed back toward Bukovci with the aim of crushing and destroying that village and enemy forces in it. The Bukovci village must be taken by nightfall on condition that we burn anything standing in our way." Now, these two sentences, General, in paragraph 2 that the villages will be burnt to the ground and in paragraph 3 that the Bukovci village must be taken by nightfall on condition that "we burn anything standing in our way," taking those two aspects of this order, General, this is an illegal order, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, this was an illegal order, and I saw this order for the first time in the courtroom here, but this order was not carried out and it was not executed. I know the terrain very well and each of the villages mentioned here, and there are villages in which there was never any fighting at all. So this order was not carried out, as I say, and point 1 of this order shows that, despite the fact that there were combat activities in the municipality of Busovaca for two days, that in Kiseljak, not even mobilisation of soldiers had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The man who issued this order, Mijo Bozic, is a man that you personally appointed to command the Ban Jelacic Brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and I really don't know the circumstances because I never discussed this document with Mijo Bozic, nor did I ever see this document before I was confronted with it here in this courtroom. But Mr. Mijo Bozic, as far as I know him, would never have been capable of implementing a document of this kind. He's not that kind of man, and I think I know him well enough to be able to say that. As I say, this order was not implemented because in some of the villages, I know each and every house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, your chief of operations, Brigadier Slavko Marin, identified both the stamp and the signature on this document as belonging to Mijo Bozic and the stamp as belonging to the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember what he identified, but I don't bring into question the fact that this is the stamp. It is, in fact, the stamp of the Ban Jelacic Brigade. That's quite true. It is the signature of the Commander Mijo Bozic, Your Honours. But I'm surprised there is no signature or initials by the author of the document, in fact. In the left-hand corner there should be the initials of the author of this document. It should be an initialled document, but in view of the villages that are quoted, which I know very well because they are from my own local community, then I believe that the person writing this order did not take into consideration all the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This order was issued, General, on the 27th of January, 1993, on a day that you yourself were in Kiseljak; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the day too when I was at the UNPROFOR headquarters at the negotiations in Kiseljak, yes. I was at the U.N. headquarters attending the negotiations. But this order was never acted upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After the negotiations, you went back to the Kiseljak barracks where Mijo Bozic and the Ban Jelacic Brigade were, and you said that you drafted Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/8, this cease-fire that was to go into effect at midnight; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The cease-fire referred to the combat activities in the area where they were going on, in fact, that is to say, part of the Zenica-Busovaca municipalities and everything that we had agreed upon with the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army and the 1st Corps of the BH army, but for the area of Kiseljak there were no combat activities whatsoever. There were no incidents there either. There was not a single Muslim house that was destroyed, let alone village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, given that the cease-fire was to come into effect at midnight on the evening of the 28th, this order seeks to have the HVO accomplish its tasks by nightfall, before the cease-fire comes into effect; isn't that right? I refer you to the last sentence in paragraph 3: "The Bukovci village must be taken by nightfall on condition that we burn anything standing in our way."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's be careful here, Mr. Kehoe. There might be a translation problem. In order 456/8A bis, I find that the French version deadline --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Midnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I find 12.00. Paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's paragraph 1, "Cessation of hostilities," Mr. President. "The cessation of hostilities be implemented and that all weapons of calibre cease firing." The deadline for that is 28 January, 1993 at 00.01. So that would be midnight of the evening going from the 27th going to the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. But there is another deadline which appears at paragraph 6 but that's not the deadline you're speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. President. That has to do with the unblocking of the road. There are several deadlines in this -- several issues covered. That is yet a different deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I do apologise, Mr. Kehoe. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, going back to Prosecutor's Exhibit 510, Bukovci village was ordered to be taken by nightfall, and this order to take Bukovci or burn it had to be accomplished before the cease-fire came into effect; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it's not, because you can see point 3 is a conditional provision. It is clear, if you read it, that the individual writing the order says that after these villages have been taken, the enemy is to be pushed back toward the village of Bukovci, that is to say, on condition that we have accomplished point 1. Then it says "by night," not by midnight. "By nightfall" means when night falls and not midnight. So the author could not have envisaged a cease-fire at all, because I myself did not know when the cease-fire would come about. I think and believe that it was proposed by Brigadier Cordy-Simpson at the meeting linked to the cease-fire, that is to say. But point 3 is quite clear. It is conditional. That means that if point 1 is implemented, then point 3 can go on and be implemented in turn. But, I repeat, this order was not implemented. It was not carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, you agree with me that the Bukovci village had to be taken by nightfall, and that event was prior to the time when the cease-fire would come into effect?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Point 3 is quite clear here. Therefore, point 3 is conditional. If point 1 is implemented, then point 3 would be put into effect, as it is stated here, by nightfall, as it states, not by midnight. But as I say, none of the points of this order were, in fact, ever carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, during the course of the conflict in Kiseljak and Busovaca -- but we'll focus on Kiseljak first. During the course of the conflict in Kiseljak in 1993, numerous Bosnian Muslim houses were burnt by HVO troops, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just a minute. We're talking about the conflict in January 1993. So tell me one house that was burnt, of a Bosniak Muslim, that is. Quote one house, because I claim that not a single house was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, the question is 1993. The question is 1993. Focus on the question. During the conflict with the Muslims in 1993, numerous Bosnian Muslim houses were burnt by HVO troops, and you sat here during the testimony of many of the witnesses that attested to that; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you are talking about the conflict from April onwards, then at that time I was blocked in Vitez and I was isolated, cut off from Kiseljak. I do know that there were features which were burnt as a result of combat operations, and I believe that in the weeks to come and months to come there were buildings that were burnt by the crime groups, groups of criminals, to cover up looting and pilferage that took part in the numerous villages of the Kiseljak municipality, but this was done successfully over a longer period of time, almost up until the signing of the Washington Agreement. It was very difficult to ascertain whether the houses were burnt by civilians or whether they had been burnt by soldiers, because the greatest problem, and that can be seen from this particular document, that is to say, document 510, that all the military conscripts on the territory of Kiseljak were civilians until they were called up to join the units. On an average, he would be a civilian for 21 days and then a soldier for the rest of the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Let us move to the next document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 677.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 677 is a military information summary of the Cheshire Regiment dated 6 February, 1993. Mr. Usher, I am interested in page 2. At the top it starts, "Two, Gornji Vakuf." That's it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As I just noted, General, this is Exhibit 677, a military information summary from the British Battalion, dated 6 February, 1993. It receipts as follows under "Gornji Vakuf": "B company reported that Gornji Vakuf was somewhat quieter than yesterday. There was a lot of small-arms fire exchanges coming from the town at approximately 09.00 hours. At 14.00 hours, three to four mortar rounds landed on the Muslim part of town with two T-55s also engaging the town. One of the T-55s was at," and it gives a grid reference. "Last night it was reported that the HVO commander Zrenko Topcic issued an ultimatum to the BiH forces to surrender their weapons to the HVO. If they, the BiH, refused he would burn the town to the ground. The next morning two petrol tankers were sighted on the high ground accompanied by a T-55 at grid reference," and it gives a grid reference. "Comment. This incident has obviously added weight to the HVO commander's threat. However, it is difficult to assess if and how he will carry out his threat. Comment ends." Now, General, it is a fact, is it not, that the HVO did burn numerous Muslim houses in Gornji Vakuf during 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're asking me about February 1993, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am asking about 1993. With this information given by the British Battalion, I am asking you, as you sit here now, it is a fact, is it not, that the HVO burned numerous Bosnian Muslim houses in the Gornji Vakuf area in 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Throughout that time and especially on the 6th of February in Kiseljak. I'm not questioning what happened in Gornji Vakuf but it is also a fact that we had two completely different situations, one in Kiseljak where I was isolated from my command and the other was in Gornji Vakuf. In Gornji Vakuf, quite obviously the conflict was ongoing and there was certain activities being performed there. In Kiseljak in June 1992 -- no, in 1993, the Bosniak Muslims were afforded every protection and there was no maltreatment at that time, abuse at that time. I do not have any precise data as to what was going on, but I do not bring into question what has just been read out from the milinfosum, that is to say, the milinfosum from the BritBat battalion. I was not in a position to have proper information myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, in 1994, when you took the office of the deputy chief of staff and, thereafter, when you took the office of chief of staff, you learned about the methods employed by the HVO in Kiseljak and that those methods employed the burning of Bosnian Muslim houses? You learned that fact, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said what was a general phenomenon. I did not receive information from my subordinates that the brigade had been given orders to burn a village or that the battalion had received or a company or platoon had received orders of that kind, but I did see that there were some burnt facilities, and this burning took place over a longer length of time, practically two years, in fact. The investigations that were conducted by the civilian and military police had difficulty in identifying whether the burning had been done by military persons or civilians, because for a time everybody was both a military individual and a civilian, depending on the period. It was the most difficult thing to identify the perpetrator. I think that there were a great many -- as there were a great many refugees at the time and the authorities were not able to see to them, they had to ensure a means of livelihood for themselves. This often included, unfortunately, looting. After looting, they would set fire to the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us return just briefly to Defence Exhibit 347, if we may. As we stay on this burning issue. Now, General, this is the order that we discussed, I believe, yesterday, or maybe prior to that time, which is the Defence exhibit from the 5th of November of 1995, where you command that all measures shall be taken to prevent setting fire to houses of eminent citizens of Muslim nationalities. All available means shall be employed to carry out this assignment and most rigorous measures shall be taken against transgressors in accordance with the military discipline regulations. Let me read to you the testimony on this score by your chief of operations, Slavko Marin, who, in October of 1993 (sic), was, in fact, stationed at HVO headquarters in Novi Travnik, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I apologise. Are you talking about October 1993? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: October of 1992 -- if I misspoke, I apologise, General. In October of 1992, during the conflict in Novi Travnik, Slavko Marin was at the HVO headquarters in Novi Travnik; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that he was at the headquarters in Novi Travnik. I can't remember the exact date, but quite possibly that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read you his testimony about these burnings that are depicted in Defence Exhibit 347. It begins on page 13165 and the question on line 15: "Q ... Houses of prominent Muslims are being burned in your municipality. A Mr. President, Mr. President, this is what I have to say regarding this document." This is concerning Defence Exhibit 347. "A ... This document was compiled on the basis of the agreement of General Merdan and Mr. Tihomir Blaskic and as a result of the cessation of hostilities between the HVO and the BH army, and it was within that conflict, which was in October, sometime around the 20th, that these houses were being burned. Muslim houses were not being set on fire if there were no combat operations there." According to Brigadier Marin, it is in the course of the conflict in Novi Travnik that HVO troops burnt Muslim houses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. What is contained in the question that my colleague said is not contained in Slavko Marin's quotation. He didn't say that the HVO burnt houses but that houses were burnt in the area where there was fighting, and that's a difference. It's the territory where there was a conflict. He never said that the HVO forces burnt the houses, so that is an assertion that does not emanate from Slavko Marin's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, it seemed to me that the quote taken from General Slavko Marin's testimony implicitly said that houses had been burned. But, Mr. Kehoe, maybe you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Slavko Marin's quote notes or did you understand it to mean that houses are being burnt and those houses are burnt during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Would you please read me that quotation once again and a little more slowly, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- because it's too fast. I'm getting the interpretation very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll read it as slowly as I possibly can, General, and if it's too fast for you, just ask me to slow down and I'll do that for you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I quote: "A Mr. President, Mr. President, this is what I have to say regarding this document. This document was compiled on the basis of the agreement of General Merdan and Mr. Tihomir Blaskic and as a result of the cessation of hostilities between the HVO and the BH army, and it is within that conflict, which was in October, sometime around the 20th, that these houses were being burned. Muslim houses were not being set on fire, if there were no combat operations there." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, have you understood that? Is it clear enough for you and was it read slowly enough for you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, this comment made by Slavko Marin is quite clear to me where he says that houses were burned where there were combat operations and where there was a conflict, that is to say, where fighting was during combat operations. However, I wish to say one thing in connection with the conflict in Novi Travnik and the burning of houses and all the crimes that were committed. Your Honours, according to the decision of the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a joint commission was set up to establish the causes and consequences of all crimes and all problems that came into being during the conflict in Novi Travnik. That commission worked until the 4th of November, 1992, that is to say, to investigate the burning of houses, the killings, et cetera. Then on the 4th of November, 1992, I received information in writing that the members of that commission from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were refusing to continue work on the investigation of the causes and consequences of the conflict in October 1992 in Novi Travnik. The commission was, therefore, forced to stop its work. I received information in writing about this, and I told Dzemo Merdan about this at the meeting on the 4th of November, 1992, asking that the members of this commission return and that the commission fully establishes what is the cause of the conflict in Novi Travnik and what the consequences of the conflict in Novi Travnik are, including all the burned buildings during that conflict. Regrettably, the commission did not complete this. I was informed in writing by Mr. Marko Prskalo about this problem, that they did not want to participate in resolving this problem, that is to say, the representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's clear, is it not, General, that Brigadier Marin believes that these houses, these Muslim houses were being burnt during the course of combat operations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and that is what it pertains to, but this order pertains to the houses of businessmen, prominent people, rich people. This order relates to what Mr. Dzemo Merdan was asking me to do, that is to say, people who have enough money. Because criminal groups were guided by profit. Ethnicity was not important for them. They were only concerned about who had money on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I know that you're focusing on a certain point, but may I, General, take you back to the explanation which you gave as to the non-completion of the work of the commission of inquiry? I gathered that your position was that the BiH refused to continue participation in the work of the commission. You spoke to Dzemo Merdan. Did he explain to you or did you, from other sources, understand why the BiH refused to continue participation in the work of the commission of inquiry?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I told Dzemo Merdan about this as well, that is to say, that the members of the commission refused to go on working, and the priority of this commission was to establish what the causes and consequences of the conflict were. Perhaps it is quite clear from the very task of the commission why the representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina refused to continue working on this commission. They were supposed to go to the very end. They were supposed to give an answer to everything that was going on in Novi Travnik, the killing of the commander in Novi Travnik, and I believe that there are reports of the commission to that effect. We saw a document yesterday, the letter of President Izetbegovic, in which he is a priorio saying who started the conflict in Novi Travnik. Perhaps he did not receive information from Dzemo Merdan on who stopped the work of the commission, but I certainly discussed this with Dzemo Merdan. It was in my interest for this commission to complete its work entirely, that is to say, to establish the causes and consequences.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Judge Shahabuddeen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you to be saying that you know that the BiH refused to continue participation in the work of the commission of inquiry. My question was whether you understood the reasons why the BiH refused to continue participation? Do you think you have given me that answer?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not have the opportunity of sharing views with the members of that commission. I did not manage to hear from them why they did not wish to continue their work, but I imagine that throwing more light on all events in that town and establishing the truth did not suit someone after all. I see no other reason, because the commission was working in Novi Travnik, the security was the same for both groups of members, and there was no reason why their work should be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. I understand this, that you were not given any reasons, but the reasons which you have now provided are the results of your own reflection; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. I did not receive any direct reasons for that, except for the information in writing that the members of the commission from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were refusing to continue working on this joint commission for Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Kehoe, I return the matter to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, in April of 1993 until you left the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, Mario Cerkez was the commander of the Viteska Brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From April, it was Mario Cerkez, but it changed. For a certain period of time, he was replaced by Vlado Juric. I think this was sometime in December 1993, and I left in '94, sometime in May. So Mario Cerkez was there from the establishment of the Vitez Brigade, the end of March or beginning of April until December '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In April, May, and June of 1993, Mario Cerkez was your subordinate as the brigade commander of the Viteska Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was a brigade that was still in the process of establishment. We started establishing it in April, May, June '93. These were the very beginnings of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let me read you the testimony of Colonel Henk Morsink, who is now a Colonel in the army of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. At that time, during 1993, I believe that Colonel Morsink was a Major. Nevertheless, he served in Bosnia at this time as part of the European Community Monitoring Mission. Let me read you a page or two of Colonel Morsink's testimony, General, beginning on 9901 with the question of my colleague, Mr. Harmon, commencing on line 10: "Q ... how were the majority of Muslim houses damaged, in your opinion? A The majority of the houses was damaged by severe fire, maybe lit with petrol or gasoline, but they were damaged by fire and definitely not by artillery fire or something else. Q Now, did you base your opinion on any conversations that you had with HVO commanders as well? A I remember a conversation quite well which happened at the joint commission Vitez with the brigade commander HVO Vitez president, Mr. Mario Cerkez, and he was very upset that the army of BiH was trying to get in new forces into Kruscica through the mountains, there's a small goat trail through the mountains, and he said that that should be stopped, and if not, he was willing to burn down all Kruscica. And I was really surprised by an outcry like that because he was an HVO officer, he was the brigade commander in the area, he was wearing his uniform, and I didn't expect an officer at all to make a statement like that. Q Was that statement made on the 24th of May, 1993, a matter of weeks after the burning of Ahmici and other villages in and around Central Bosnia? A I do not recall the exact date, but it was made several weeks after all the villages in the area had been burnt. Q Did you take that threat of Mario Cerkez seriously? A Well, he said it in a very clear way, and he was on duty when he said it. He was an active member of the local joint commission. Q Now, in your opinion, could all the burning that you've just described that you saw been committed --" Excuse me. Let me reread that again. "Q Now, in your opinion, could all the burning that you've just described that you saw been committed by uncontrolled elements? A I do not believe that all the burning was done by uncontrolled elements since it was done in a systematic way all more or less in the same time. Q In your opinion, Colonel Morsink, was Colonel Blaskic aware of this illegal HVO practice? A He must have been aware of it since it was in his area of operation, and it was -- it was mentioned in several meetings where his people were present. Q So complaints were made about it at the joint commissions where his designees were present? A That's correct. Q Did you ever, at any time while you were in Central Bosnia, ever hear of any HVO soldier being punished or disciplined for burning down a Muslim house? A None whatsoever. Q In your opinion, Colonel Morsink, why did the HVO engage in this practice? A I think it was one way to clear the area of all Muslims." Now, General, based on that testimony from Colonel Morsink, we have before the Court at least two of your brigade commanders, one issuing an order and one making a statement concerning the burning down of Bosnian Muslim houses; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is possible that he made such a statement, but Muslim houses in Kruscica were not burned, never. From the very first day of the conflict, Kruscica was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If any houses were burned, then it was only Croat houses that were burned in that area. But allow me to say in connection with that zone that only one village was burned by a military unit and that is the village of Ahmici. The other burning went on for weeks, months, even throughout the year, and mostly at night by perpetrators unknown, where it is very difficult to establish whether the perpetrator was a civilian or a member of the military. In that area, there were 35.000 refugees who were looting these houses so that they could make a living for themselves. Usually after this looting these houses were burned. I personally issued orders not only in accordance with document 347, let me just mention document 318, document 338, 359, 361, 370, 371, and 376. So I even issued orders that may be absurd. In 359, I forbid the burning of houses. I forbid something that is forbidden bylaw, but the problem was that the situation that we were in, that is to say, of a total encirclement, that I focused on the front line and security affairs were left to the civilian police, the military police, and the security service. At Grbavica, a refugee was killed only because he tried to steal some goods that he needed perhaps in order to survive that particular day, but it was impossible to stop a mob. You could only start shooting at all of them now, the police or whoever. I know that I had said in another village there should be protection, but this protection was not efficient enough. I know that houses were systematically burnt throughout this period but by perpetrators unknown in order to conceal looting. Those were the rumours that were going around most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You say it was done "by perpetrators unknown," General. Well, let me direct your attention to the 17th of April of 1993, a day after Ahmici was burnt, and you told us during your direct-examination, to questions by Mr. Nobilo, that the HVO had troops in Loncari. If you don't recall that, check your chronology.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I shall. The 17th of April, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please do. I refer you to your testimony, if that would be of any assistance, which is at page 18727 -- I apologise. Excuse me. That's right, 18727, where you note that Marin is to ask Cerkez to contact the soldiers of the Busovaca Brigade in Loncari. Do you see that in your chronology, General? Again this is, of course, on the 17th of April. My colleague has just noted for me the specific hour that this message was sent and it was at 18.48 -- excuse me, 18.58.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I found that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the troops from the Busovaca Brigade or the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade were in Loncari on the 17th of April, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that it is so, because we asked that contact be established with these soldiers from the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade in Loncari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This particular brigade is a brigade that is in your direct chain of command; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That brigade was under my direct command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if you wanted to break now or just continue on? I'll continue on. I thought you were looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's true, I often look at the clock during this trial, but not particularly today or right now. We've started a bit late, so I see on the other hand that Judge Rodrigues has a question to put to the witness. We can go on for a few minutes. Maybe if General Blaskic had wanted to look for a number of documents I would have taken a break now, but we can work for another ten minutes, if that's agreeable to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, as long as Your Honour wants to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, you told us that you had become aware of the fact that some Muslim houses had been burnt. You also said that criminal groups had been responsible for those acts, not your soldiers. You also told us that you issued a number of orders. Is that what you said? Have I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The burning of houses, I said that that took place most often in order to conceal looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But is that true? I mean, have you actually said what I have tried to put to you? Are you in agreement with what I've said?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not preclude the possibility of there having been a single soldier who looted a house and burned it. There were perhaps soldiers or perhaps there were civilians, but that was the major problem, whether a house was burned by soldier or civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: My question is the following: What was the use of issuing orders meant for your soldiers when you knew that these soldiers were not responsible for the burnt houses?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The greatest problem was to establish who was responsible for the burning. I issued orders in order to warn them that this should not be done and that this was a criminal act to commit such acts. I issued orders so that these orders would go down the chain of command to each and every soldier. Most of these burnings took place at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Did you think about sending your troops on the ground in order for them to prevent these burnings to take place, because it seems to me that at the end, your troops were much more powerful than those criminal groups that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sometime around the end of October 1993, the soldiers were stronger and then there were hardly burnings but until that time these groups were stronger. Of course I thought about it. Well, in Donje Veceriska it was at my request that a guard was placed to guard houses, and it was at my request that the civilian police secured Grbavica and took care of the houses so that they would not be looted and burned. Krizancevo Selo, which is a Croat village, Your Honour, it was burnt in December 1993. It was burnt by Croats, not Muslims. The problem was that there was a large number of refugees who could not be taken care of, from a social point of view. Thirty thousand refugees is a problem for a state, and to make it possible for them to survive the winter. There was famine as well. Looting was there to conceal -- burning was there to conceal the looting of houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you noted for us that the troops of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade were in Loncari on the 17th of April, 1993, and I would like to read to you some excerpts from the testimony of Witness Q. This testimony, Mr. President, was given in open session. However, there were certain measures taken to protect the identity of Witness Q, but we can read this transcript in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. If it was done within a public hearing, there's no reason for us to go into private session. I see that the witness was protected. The only measure we have to take is not to the witness, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. This starts at line 6. This individual is from Loncari and living in Loncari, talking about the events of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counsel, do you have a page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, counsel, 5158, line 6: "I saw the HVO military approaching the house." Carrying down to line 14: "I carried out my 11-month-old child and I was barefoot. I was holding my daughter with my other hand. They ordered us then to go to my sister-in-law's house, and that is where we were standing, in front of her house, and an HVO soldier entered into my sister-in-law's house. He had a canister in his hand (sic)." Excuse me. It says in his "house." "He had a canister in his house. There was fuel, maybe some petrol, in it. I heard him banging around the house, turning things over, breaking things." Turn to the next page, 5159, beginning on line 1. "He said that I could but I had to come back right away. So I went in, and I took them, and I came right out, and I already saw that he had taken the canister and he was pouring whatever it was, it could have been oil or fuel, but he set my sister's house on fire. Then he also did it to my mother-in-law's house. I saw it burning. "Then the HVO soldiers told us to go in front of them. We went to the mekteb and there were a lot of people there." Completing this going down to line 25: "After awhile we saw that everything was on fire." Now, General, this burning was done by troops under your direct command, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This burning was committed by an individual who has his name and surname. Troops under my control never received approval or an order to do something like that. On the contrary. They received opposite orders. Already on the 17th of April, I ordered, in document 318, I think under point 4: "Collect information about the protagonists of house burning and other facilities." So I'm already issuing an order that I be given information. I assert that there is not a single information of this kind that I received without my having reacted to it in keeping with my responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this particular event, the burning of Loncari, took place a day after the village of Ahmici was completely burnt; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is right, but we are talking about a specific event and a specific building, and Loncari was a front line. It went through half of the village. This was in the later period. So the front line went through the village. I asked that measures be taken and that this be prevented, but I also asked for them to report back to me. 318, 359, all these documents, these are documents that are evidence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I must say I don't understand your answer, General Blaskic. You speak of strategy in the village of Loncari. Do you want to say that if the houses were burnt it was within the framework of a combat operation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The house that the Honourable Prosecutor spoke of a few moments ago was not burned down in combat operations, but he said that the village of Loncari was burned down and that's what I'm referring to, that the front line went through half of the village of Loncari. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, when Ahmici was burnt down there was no front line through the village of Ahmici, was there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that the only village that was burnt down by a military unit was Ahmici. That is a crime, and that was committed by a military unit. It is certain that this cannot be said as it was done in other areas, one house by one within an entire year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, the village of Loncari was burnt to the ground on the 17th of April, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have such information that it was burnt to the ground, but I do know that this was where the front line was, and I already said that in these various documents that are evidence, I asked for information to be sent by subordinates to me on the burning of these houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's try to be clear so that the witness can give us a useful answer. Loncari was completely burned or was it the witness's house that was completely burnt? What is it you're putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The witness testified, on line 25, Mr. President, page 5159: "After awhile we saw that everything was on fire."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay. Right. So it's on the basis of this testimony, General Blaskic, that Mr. Kehoe is putting to you that it was not a single house that was burnt but the whole village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, on the next page the witness then describes how the witness went back into the witness's house --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, may I remind you that General Blaskic is now a witness. He is the accused but also the witness. I was putting the question to him, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, this is not a contradictory debate right now. You will have your right to rejoinder and you will put your question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's fine, but I object to counsel stating that the record is something, in a language the witness cannot review or consult, when it is wrong and it is misleading. That is what I object to.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Prosecutor read a text to me where the witness speaks about his house that was burned down. I did not get anything else. The question was related to that text, to the best of my understanding. Perhaps the interpretation I got was not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: May I remind you, General, that it was -- I want everything to be very clear to you, General Blaskic. May I remind you that I was the one to ask for that detailed explanation by the Prosecution because I wanted things to be clear. It will be the responsibility of your Defence counsel, within their right to rejoinder, to make further statements on that particular issue and, also, you will have more time to look at that particular testimony. Right now I'm concentrating on what Mr. Kehoe has been saying, i.e. that the village of Loncari was completely burned down. Right now I think it would be a good idea to take a 15-minute break, because we have a long morning of work before us. This will enable us, among other things, to take good notice of what the witness said so that we can go on in a useful manner. We'll have a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Mr. Kehoe, I hope that the witness has had enough time to go over the document we were looking at a moment ago. Would you like to put your question to him once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Before I do that, in light of comments made prior to the break, I'd like to continue on just briefly with Witness Q's testimony concerning Loncari on the 17th of April, and I am referring to page 5160, beginning on line 7. "A I went to my house to see whether there was anything I could find him so that they --" Talking about her children "-- could eat. I went with my sister-in-law, we were in great fear because everything was on fire, terrible shooting. I went to my house which had already been burnt down. There was nothing that I could find there. I went to my mother-in-law's, to her house, and that house was also on fire, but a found a T-shirt which I put over my nose and my mouth so that I could enter the house, even though it was on fire, it was filled with smoke, but I had to go in and see if I could find anything for my children, for the other children, but no, there was nothing there either. Everything had burned down. There was just a bag with clothing which had started to burn. I took that and I brought it out. I then returned to the mekteb, because everything had burned down and there was nothing to be found there. So for awhile, we were there in fear, and after that, we decided to go in the direction of Vrhovine, and then whatever the fate would give us, whatever would happen to us, because there was nothing for us there, it was over, everything had burned down."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, those were your troops under your command that burnt down that village. Did you go and visit Loncari and see the damage and the burning that they had wrought on that village?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not receive this particular piece of information that I have just heard here. I learnt of it here in the Tribunal for the first time. The information that I received from my subordinate commanders was that there was fighting in the village of Loncari. I never received this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question for you was did you go to Loncari after the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not because I received information that there were combat operations, and I went where I was given information that the fighting was the strongest and that I was most needed. I never got any information until I came here to the courtroom. Had I known about these events and had I received reports about that from my subordinates, quite certainly, I would have gone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How far is the village of Loncari from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can give you an approximation, perhaps 10 to 12 kilometres. Although with combat operations going on, in wartime, that is, the distance doesn't mean a great deal because it depends, first of all, whether you have information and what the priorities are. I behaved according to the information that I would receive from my subordinates, and the reports I received told me that there was fighting not only in Loncari but at almost 25 or 30 other places as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Loncari is in the Busovaca municipality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Loncari is in the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let us move ahead. On the 19th of April, were the military police still attached to you for combat activities?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the testimony of Ibrahim Nuhagic from the village of Ocehnici in Busovaca. I read to you from page 5217 concerning the events of the 19th, starting on line 14: "A We were there until February, and then we were let go, we were allowed to go back home and most of us decided to return to our homes. We were told that nobody would bother us. Until April 1993, it was like that and so we even started to work on our fields. Sometime in the afternoon, the HVO soldiers simply walked in the village. We had nothing at that time and there was nobody to put up any resistance and we could not do anything, because we were under HVO control. They started burning and killing whoever they could reach." On page 5222, the witness, on line 3, notes that this event took place on the 19th of April, and on page 5235, line 20: "Q Mr. Nuhagic, did you also learn that the actual attack on your village was ordered by Pasko Ljubicic? A I learned that Pasko Ljubicic was the leader of the group." Now, Pasko Ljubicic, General, is the same commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion who participated with his troops in the attack on Ahmici; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but that military police was attached to me. I did not issue the order for attack on the village of Ocehnici. According to information received by me for the 19th of April, the combat activities were taking place in the Busovaca municipality region, and we were exposed to the strongest possible attack in the whole of the war. It was the day when we had the greatest losses and the heaviest fighting. I spoke about the system of attachment, that that meant retaining a dual line chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the whole village of Ocehnici was burnt to the ground, wasn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard the testimony here in the courtroom. I do not bring that testimony into question, but on the 19th of April, I did not receive any information about the burning of the village of Ocehnici. What I did receive was information about combat activities in the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This village was burnt to the ground by troops that were under your command; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the troops, if you're talking about the military police, were attached to me. Therefore, I did have the right to give them assignments, but I never issued an assignment of that kind. They could have received an assignment of that kind from their direct superiors, which was the head office of the military police and their superiors in Mostar. When a unit is attached, it retains its structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us return to another report, and we are going to focus back and go back to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can, Mr. Usher, I'd like to hand this report out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 678, 678A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this is a report dated the 2nd of March, 1993, some six weeks prior to the events that took place in Ahmici and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the precise date of that document, Mr. Kehoe? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The 2nd of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: March. I see. Thank you very much. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a mixed committee from both the Bosnian Muslims and from the HVO concerning -- this is a "Mixed Committee for the Registry of Destroyed and Damaged Buildings" concerning the Municipality of Busovaca. "Report: On 28 February 1993 and 1 and 2 March 1993, the Mixed Committee for the Registry of Destroyed and Damaged buildings /illegible/ war operations visited the territory under HVO control and concluded the following: "1. In the inspected territories (D. Solakovici, town of Busovaca, Buselji, Podkula, Sajkovici, Kovacevac) the Committee noted the damage of 112 buildings. Of that number, 53 were burned down and the rest were damaged and destroyed. /several words illegible/. 17 buildings can /illegible/ minor repairs /illegible/. Destroyed and damaged business premises /illegible/ can be repaired promptly." The first section, and let us go through this, General, deals with torched facilities. The first name is illegible, but the last name "Causevic," is that a Muslim name, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Ekmescic," is that a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Hamdo Ibreljic," a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To the bottom of that page, looking at all those names that you can recognise, all of those are Muslim names, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes of course, because it was probably a Muslim village in which the committee went to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next page and start from the top. Virtually all of those names are Muslim names, aren't they, if not all of them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not all of them are those names, but most of them are Muslim names, as far as I was able to look through them, but did you have any other question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. How many are not Muslim names? Tell us the names.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Safradin Anto, Satradin Anto once again, Safradin Milenko, a weekend cottage owner Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the Safradin name could very well be a mixed-marriage name; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Safradin is a name -- that is to say, it is a surname. The name is Anto and the second first name is Anto, so I was guided by the first name. The third Safradin Milenko, that is true, that name again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, continue on that sheet. We have three potentially non-Muslim houses burnt. Just continue on that list on page 2.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On page 4 I see a property owned by Bilic Boro from Busovaca. I think that the name "Boro" is not a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, those four names that you talk about being Croat names, the rest of these properties that were destroyed, burnt, and destroyed in part and whole, and burnt, virtually all of these properties Bosnian Muslim properties in the municipality of Busovaca; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In this document that is right. In point 1 it says: "In areas where the committee checked the facilities." I'm looking at this document for the first time. I never had occasion to see it previously. It is a document written by the civilian authorities. But the mixed committee of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, led by international monitors and UNPROFOR, also sent out their own reports and listed -- made up lists of the properties destroyed or damaged. I insisted that this work be continued for us to be able to ascertain the real state of affairs and the consequences of the January conflict. Also on page 4, it is stated that the committee did not complete its work and that it would continue in the course of March 1993. The only other thing, the stamp is once again a civilian authority stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the stamp that is on there is an HVO stamp; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is the civilian authority. That's precisely what I said. The civilian authorities, which after every conflict, set up parallel committees of their own which would go and make lists of the facilities and repair the properties for people to be able to take up residence there, because all those who were left had to live somewhere. The civilian authorities functioned throughout. They would make up lists of this kind and repair destroyed properties. Parallel to that was the mixed commission of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone, with Mr. Nakic and Mr. Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you noted that this is a civilian document but the heading of this document, does it not say the "HVO command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone"? Does it not say that at the top of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's the fax line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about. The fax, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, with your fax number. I'm talking about -- maybe I wasn't clear enough. I apologise, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The fax number at the top is the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, with your telephone number. Now you've noted that you've never seen this document before but it was, in fact, either sent from -- apparently sent from your headquarters.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I had not seen this document and I say that again. I never saw the document. It is a document of a civilian service, and I believe it was received by Mr. Franjo Nakic, who was a member on behalf of the Operative Zone, a member of the joint committee. We can see that the document was sent to the 3rd Corps and received by the 3rd Corps. It states exactly the number. I can see this is a correspondence between Franjo Nakic and Dzemo Merdan, in fact, who were the representatives of the joint committee. This is a partial -- these data were combined by Dzemo Merdan and Franjo Nakic, and was presented to me, and the commander of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Thebault, and Colonel Stewart at the meetings of the joint committee and the joint command in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, aside from this report are you aware of any other reports that deal with this destruction of buildings, homes, and businesses in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I spoke about the documents at the meetings that I attended when they were presented to us, when this kind of information was presented to us. Everything that happened in the villages of the Busovaca municipality, the joint committee would collect information and data. It would systematise that and at the meetings of the joint command those data were presented by Franjo Nakic and Dzemo Merdan. I never saw this document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't think any of this is contested, so I think you can move forward, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, with regard to this particular document, of course, we are talking about damage to buildings and destruction of buildings, as it notes in the outset, in territory under HVO control. This morning, starting in Busovaca or, excuse me, in Kiseljak with the Mijo Bozic order to burn, and in Gornji Vakuf with a record of the commander there to burn, and then with Mario Cerkez's threat to burn, and with all the burning that was going around the Central Bosnia area, my question for you, General, is: It would appear clear that there was a concerted policy of the HVO to burn down the houses of Bosnian Muslims, isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already said that there was never an order issued to any single unit, nor did I receive information that a unit had come to a village in an organised fashion and burnt down the buildings. The situation in Gornji Vakuf was fighting in a populated area. I do not have information on that. In Kiseljak, the commands issued by Bozic was not put into effect. I myself, unfortunately, did not receive information apart from the information related to Ahmici when I did, in fact, react. As far as this kind of report is concerned, they were dual reports, that is to say, the members of the joint committee would submit reports to us, and according to the chairman dictating the tempo, that is how I and the commander of the 3rd Corps reacted, most frequently by issuing orders that there be a cessation to actions leading to destruction and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, I understand the question to be this: Apart altogether from the question what orders were given to what units and whether any orders were given to burn houses, do you know, as a fact, whether Muslim houses were being burnt by the HVO? If you knew that, would you say that there was a coherent or concerted policy for the HVO to burn down Muslim houses? That's how I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not aware of the fact that an orchestrated policy existed for Muslim houses to be burnt down because, Your Honour, in January 1993 when I was in Kiseljak, there is not a single Muslim -- there was not a single Muslim house that had been burnt but Croatian houses had been burnt in Bilalovac, but that was no reason for an HVO soldier to burn down a single Muslim house in Kiseljak. We do not have any report of this kind from Bilalovac because the joint committee led by Dzemo Merdan and Franjo Nakic, that is to say, the supreme committee, was not able to enter Bilalovac. But the houses were, nevertheless, burnt. So that no policy existed. I had my doubts that among those burning houses there were soldiers too, but I did not receive information. For example, the concrete case of Loncari mentioned and the event that is profoundly moving, the testimony by Witness Q, I had heard Witness Q here in this Tribunal, I did receive information there was fighting there, combat operations there, and at meetings -- I believe that the minutes exist of this, of the 25th of February, asked that a joint committee go to tour all the villages and to collect information of this kind for us to be able to ask the assistance of the civilian authorities to put things right. Sometime around the 5th of February, there was some ten properties that had been burnt. In the period later on, there was more burning. This went on for days, and weeks, and even months. As I said, the burning usually took place during the night. Apart from that, we had 35.000 refugees without anything in the world to their name. I was watching the Kosovo reports. They didn't come with tractors. They came carrying little bags in their hands. They had to withdraw with because of the civil war between the HVO and the TO. The Gornji Vakuf area is quite different from the Vitez and Kiseljak regions. In each environment, completely different things were going on all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, during the course of the time when you were the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, can you give us the name of one HVO soldier who was arrested for burning down a Muslim house, one?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you see, several days ago I discussed this question. I spoke about the issue. There is no commander of the Operative Group who in his notebook had the name jotted down of one particular soldier. In the former JNA, that is to say, I had to work several levels lower. I had to see what commanders of the battalions were doing. But I was setting up a system by which to prevent that burning. First all, by prohibiting activities of this kind and been cautioning people that this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, you've told us about all this, but here the question is very direct. Can you give us the name of one HVO soldier who was arrested for burning down a Muslim house? That is the question. Can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Soldiers. If -- that is to say, if information was received, then that particular soldier was prosecuted. A criminal report would come in and then he would be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, could you please try to answer the question put to you? Can you name one HVO soldier who was arrested for burning down a Muslim house? Maybe you know. Maybe you don't know. Maybe the system did not imply that you would not be informed of such an act. But this is not semantics. Could you try to answer the questions put to you? Can you give us the name of one HVO soldier who was arrested for burning down a Muslim house? That's it. That's all we're asking of you for the moment being, at least.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the moment I don't have the name and surname of any soldier for me to be able to answer that question, but I do know that disciplinary measures were taken and that perpetrators were punished, but I don't have a list of all the soldiers and conscripts here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Then, I guess, during their right to rejoinder your Defence counsels will make that point once again. All right. Mr. Kehoe, you can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you mentioned a different issue, and that was the issue of the discipline. You, as the commanding officer of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, had had overall responsibility over the military disciplinary courts, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Over the military disciplinary courts? I did have powers over them, and in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, I believe throughout the HVO, I believe it is -- or, rather, if you look at the entire HVO, I'm sure that military disciplinary courts were first formed in Central Bosnia. I always sought the advice of lawyers, and I wanted my superior -- my subordinate officers to become familiar with the work of military disciplinary courts. We studied this together, and we had lectures organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, we have received numerous documents from the Defence concerning the imposition of military discipline, and none of those documents contain any discipline meted out to a soldier for burning of a Muslim house. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: But I think that in the rules on military discipline it says quite clearly when disciplinary action is taken and who takes disciplinary action. I think that this is something that is quite clear in the rules and regulations or, rather, burning houses is not a disciplinary offence. This is a crime. The way we were trained, the way I was trained at the military academy, that is a far graver thing and one is subject to the law on criminal procedure, whereas disciplinary action is taken by platoon commanders, company commanders, battalion commanders, brigade commanders, and commanders of Operative Zones, and they have a certain span, depending on the disciplinary offence committed. It's not a disciplinary offence if a soldier comes up and burns a house down. That is a crime, and there is a crime investigation service within the military police to take care of that. They are supposed to submit a criminal report to the district military court. I do not have jurisdiction in criminal procedure, according to the law on criminal procedure, unless I get the name and surname of the soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What department, what criminal department, are you talking about, General, please?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the perpetrator of a crime is a soldier, then it is the crime department of the military police that looks into this, that is to say, that this kind of a department exists within the military police, and they prevent and investigate crime. It is a disciplinary offence if a soldier gets drunk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Where can this department be found? Where is it located?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was attached to the 4th Battalion of the military police. The commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police had a co-worker of his who is head of the department of the crime investigation service, and he only deals with crimes, whereas the discipline of soldiers is something that the platoon commander is supposed to deal with. He has a book, we called it the report book. That is where it says that Marko Markovic, a soldier, got drunk, and the consequences were not very grave, that is to say, the soldier got drunk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, can we try to make this as clear as possible? We, the Judges, are relying on your questions and maybe also on the Defence counsel's questions to well understand this issue, because the witness is putting to us a very theoretical theory, and what we, the Judges, are interested in is the translation, in fact, of this theory when a house is burnt by a soldier who is under the orders of a certain commandment, we want to know exactly what is supposed to happen. Can you try to put a very precise question to the witness on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, it is a fact, is it not, that if a soldier commits a crime, there are two available punishments he can receive: He can receive a criminal punishment and he can receive a military disciplinary punishment from you, which includes removal from military service. He can receive both of them, can't he? If you want to examine the Narodni Lists on the issue, we can do that as well.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was trained and I worked in a different way all my life. I can give a brief answer to that. If a soldier commits a crime, and if I have the name and surname of this person, Marko Markovic, a soldier, committed a crime, then I inform the crime service of the military police or I, myself, file a criminal report with the district military prosecutor at the district military court. Then it is the prosecutor in the military court who decides, irrespective of me, whether he is going to prosecute or not. If he is not going to initiate criminal proceedings, then the prosecutor takes this file and returns it to me and says, "This soldier, Marko Markovic, is supposed to receive disciplinary punishment of 60 days," but that is the decision of the prosecutor, if he committed a crime. Just one more thing. What would it be like if a soldier burned a house down, committed a crime, if his platoon commander gave him three days in custody? I've never heard of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer Your Honours to Article 29 of the Narodni Lists -- this is not the Narodni Lists; this is the Rules on Military Discipline of the Narodni Lists which reflect that: "When an officer establishes that a breach of military discipline is also a punishable act, the case shall be handed to the authorised prosecutor through official channels. If it is in the interest of the service, the officer shall also undertake measures to initiate proceedings," disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you would agree that removing soldiers who burn Bosnian Muslim houses from military service is in the interests of the HVO, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, certainly. As far as the removal of soldiers who burn down houses are concerned, you have my orders of the 17th of January when I'm asking for names, I want names to be identified, and I want to get rid of such soldiers. But, Your Honours, it is very important to understand this, to see what a disciplinary infraction is, what a disciplinary offence is, and what a crime is.
